title: How to Dominate Your Common Core Supply Needs with DonorsChoose.org
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that teachers should stop personally bankrolling their classrooms and instead use DonorsChoose.org to fund the materials their curriculum needs. He frames this as both a practical fix and a mission, since schooling improves only when responsibility is spread beyond teachers alone. Drawing on six years of experience and over $6,000 in funded requests, including class sets of demanding novels, he shows the ambitious reading expectations he holds for ninth graders are achievable without personal expense. He then lays out five tactics: think small, exploit funding opportunities, automate Facebook updates, wait when a project is within $100 of funding, and always present opportunity rather than guilt. The piece is a concrete, experience-based guide to a resource problem that many teachers silently absorb.
points: Teachers who buy their own supplies undercut the larger goal of shifting responsibility for schooling onto the wider public.
Smaller projects fund far more reliably, so a big classroom vision should be broken into a series of sub-$400 requests.
Matching a project essay to a funding opportunity's stated theme can turn a seemingly unrelated book order into a funded one.
Automated social updates and patience near the finish line leverage donors who prefer completing almost-funded projects.
Framing a request as joining a classroom on a mission, not as a guilt trip, is the principle Stuart calls key.
quotes: For schooling to get better in the US, we've got to shift the responsibility from teachers alone to every last American. You taking on every classroom expense isn't achieving that end.
I need to prove each year that teenagers will joyfully rise to ridiculously demanding expectations.

DonorsChoose projects that cost less than $400 are way more likely to get funded than those above $400. Similarly, those that cost less than $200 are way more likely still, and it's almost impossible not to get a $100 project funded.
Funding opportunities are crucial for lessening the amount of dollars you’ll need to raise from folks in your community.
Every teacher I know who has tried this (including me) has been stunned at the distant acquaintances who will come out of the woodwork and give money to your project. It’s simply amazing.

The last thing you want to do is have people associate your classroom with a guilt trip. No matter how bad off your school or your students or you are, I highly recommend framing every DonorsChoose project you create as an opportunity to join a classroom on a mission.
